verses.note: Whatever its original horizon, the verse refuses to treat Sheol as the last word for one who belongs to God. Interpreters differ on whether David hoped for rescue from an early death or for life beyond death; the psalm's language opens toward the second.

The saints are called ‘those who had fallen asleep’, the biblical way of speaking of the faithful dead as awaiting resurrection. The verses show bodily resurrection as the hope for the dead, not an escape from the body, which is why Christians have been cautious about building detailed doctrines of the state between death and resurrection on this passage.

Luke describes death as the spirit leaving and life as the spirit returning, the same language he uses when Jesus commits his spirit to the Father (23:46) and Stephen asks Jesus to receive his (Acts 7:59). The verse supports the biblical picture of the person continuing beyond death, though it says nothing about where the girl's spirit had been.

The saying has been drawn into debates about the state of the dead, especially purgatory. Roman Catholic tradition has seen in it a support for purification after death; Protestant and many other interpreters read it only as a parable of urgent reconciliation. The verse itself stresses the urgency of settling accounts, and the wider teaching of Scripture must decide the rest.

Lazarus is taken to Abraham's side at death, not at a later resurrection. The verse pictures the righteous dead received at once into rest and fellowship, which is why Christian readers have linked it with Jesus' promise to the criminal (23:43).

The rich man is conscious, remembers, speaks, and suffers before any final resurrection. How literally to take the flame, the finger, and the tongue is debated, but the verse presents personal existence continuing after death with its moral outcome already felt.

The chasm pictures a separation after death that cannot be crossed. Whatever else the imagery borrows from Jewish pictures of compartments in the realm of the dead (1 Enoch 22), its point is finality: death fixes the outcome of a life.

Readers differ on what ‘all live to him’ implies for the time before the resurrection. Many see here the conviction that the dead in God are already alive in his presence, as Jesus promised the dying criminal paradise today (23:43). Others read it chiefly as a guarantee of the future resurrection, the patriarchs being alive to God because he will certainly raise them. Both readings agree that death does not sever God's people from him.

Read in its natural sense, the verse promises a dying man conscious fellowship with Christ on the day of his death, before the resurrection of the body. It does not describe the place in detail, and Christians differ on how to speak of it, but it is a principal text for the church's confession that those who die in Christ are with him.

Jesus dies committing his spirit to the Father's keeping. The verse, with verse 43, grounds the Christian confidence that death does not put the person beyond God's care, and Christians from Stephen onward have prayed its words at the hour of death (Acts 7:59).

Amillennial readers see in this verse the state of believers between death and resurrection: the souls of the martyrs are alive with Christ and share his reign now, while their bodies wait for the resurrection at the end. On this reading the verse answers the cry of 6:9-11 by showing the martyrs already enthroned.
